questions.prompt: Four eval runs score 70, 90, 80 and 80. What are the mean and the variance (dividing by n)?

options.explanation: The mean is right, but the runs are not all equal. Variance is 0 only when every value equals the mean.
10 is the biggest distance from the mean, not the variance. Variance squares each distance first, then takes the mean of the squares: 200 ⁄ 4 = 50.
75 is the mean of 70 and 80 only. The mean adds all four runs and divides by 4: 320 ⁄ 4 = 80.
Right. The sum is 320, so the mean is 320 ⁄ 4 = 80. The squared distances are 100, 100, 0 and 0, so the variance is 200 ⁄ 4 = 50.

questions.prompt: An agent passes 90% of single trials. Using Anthropic's pass^k idea, what is the chance that it passes all 2 of 2 trials?

options.text: 90%, because each trial has the same chance.
options.explanation: Each trial has 90%, but both must pass. Steps that must all happen multiply, so the chance drops below 90%.
Right. pass^k is the probability that all k trials succeed: 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81. Anthropic's own example is 0.75³ ≈ 42%.
99% is the chance that at least one of the two trials passes: 1 − 0.1 × 0.1. Anthropic calls that pass@k (at least one success in k attempts), not pass^k.
A probability can never be above 1. Adding 0.9 + 0.9 is the wrong rule for two events that must both happen.

questions.prompt: Your old prompt scores 80 on average, and its runs spread about 14 points (standard deviation). A new prompt scores 83 in one run. What is the best next step?

options.text: Ship the new prompt, because 83 is higher than 80.
options.explanation: A 3-point gap is far smaller than a 14-point spread. One run of 83 could easily come from the old prompt too.

options.text: Drop the new prompt, because one run proves it is worse.
options.explanation: One run proves little in either direction. The data so far doesn't show it is worse; it doesn't show anything yet.

options.text: Run more trials of both prompts and compare the means.
options.explanation: Right. The gap is smaller than the spread, so it is weak evidence. The mean of n runs has a spread √n times smaller, so more runs give a fairer comparison.

options.text: Set temperature to 0, so one run is enough.
options.explanation: The Claude glossary says that even at temperature 0, identical inputs may produce different outputs across API calls. You still need more than one run.
